items.title: Getting PyTorch to Actually Use Your RTX 5090: A Complete WSL2 Setup Guide for Blackwell (sm_120)
items.content:
From a broken Windows pip install to a fully working PyTorch 2.12 build on CUDA 12.9 inside WSL2 — every failure, every fix, and every command.

The Problem Nobody Warns You About

You buy an RTX 5090. You install PyTorch. You run your training script. It works — sort of. The GPU shows up in nvidia-smi, tensors move to CUDA without errors, and you feel like everything is fine.

It is not fine.

What is actually happening is that PyTorch is falling back to a compatibility mode that does not use the Blackwell architecture properly. The RTX 5090 is a Compute Capability 12.0 GPU (sm_120). Every stable PyTorch release as of early 2026 was compiled for architectures up to sm_90 (Hopper). When PyTorch encounters sm_120 it either raises a warning and partially degrades, or throws:

CUDA error: no kernel image is available for execution on the device

This means the compiled CUDA kernels in the PyTorch wheel have no binary for your GPU. The GPU is present but fundamentally unusable for deep learning operations.

This post documents the complete journey from that error to a working PyTorch 2.12.0 build with full sm_120 support, compiled from source inside WSL2 on Ubuntu 24.04 with CUDA 12.9.

Why the Windows Path Fails

The natural first instinct is to fix this on Windows, where most researchers keep their projects. There are three approaches on Windows and all of them fail:

Approach 1: Standard pip install

The stable PyTorch wheel (cu124) does not include sm_120 kernels. You get the silent degradation or the kernel image error described above.

Approach 2: PyTorch nightly cu135

PyTorch nightly builds for Linux include sm_120 support. Windows wheels for cu135 and cu136 are not published. The index URL exists but returns no matching wheel for Windows:

ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement torch

Approach 3: Community builds (cu128.nv)

A custom Hugging Face build (torch-2.6.0+cu128.nv) does work on Windows and was the working solution for a period. However it is an unofficial build, not maintained long term, and introduces its own DLL dependency issues on machines without the right Visual C++ redistributables installed.

The conclusion is straightforward: building PyTorch with proper sm_120 support on Windows is not a supported path. WSL2 is.

Setting Up WSL2

WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux version 2) runs a real Linux kernel inside a lightweight VM on Windows. NVIDIA’s drivers expose the GPU through to WSL2 via a passthrough layer. From Linux’s perspective you have a real CUDA-capable GPU.

Prerequisites

• Windows 11 or Windows 10 build 19041+

• NVIDIA driver 525.85 or newer on Windows (the Linux driver inside WSL2 is provided automatically)

• WSL2 enabled (not WSL1)

Open WSL2

Press Win + R, type wsl, press Enter. Or open Windows Terminal and select Ubuntu from the dropdown.

You land as root. Always switch to your user account immediately:

su — yourusername

Verify the GPU is visible inside WSL2:

nvidia-smi

You should see your RTX 5090 listed with Driver Version from Windows (e.g. 576.88) and CUDA Version 12.9. If this fails, your WSL2 GPU passthrough is not configured — ensure you are running WSL2 not WSL1, and that your NVIDIA driver version is recent enough.

The CUDA Toolkit Trap on Ubuntu 24.04

This is the most important section because it is where most builds silently fail or produce a GPU that appears to work but does not.

Ubuntu 24.04’s default apt repository includes a package called nvidia-cuda-toolkit. Do not install it. It installs CUDA 12.0, which predates Blackwell support entirely. nvcc from this package will reject sm_120:

nvcc fatal : Unsupported gpu architecture ‘compute_120’

The second trap is NCCL. If you previously installed NCCL from NVIDIA’s repo, you may find a version like libnccl2 2.29.7–1+cuda13.2 sitting on your system while your toolkit is CUDA 12.0 or 12.6. This version mismatch causes linker errors deep in the build that are difficult to diagnose.

The Correct CUDA Installation Path

Remove any existing CUDA toolkit installed via apt:

sudo apt remove -purge -y nvidia-cuda-toolkit nvidia-cuda-dev nvidia-cuda-gdb \ nvidia-cuda-toolkit-doc libcudart12 sudo apt autoremove -y

Add NVIDIA’s official CUDA repository for Ubuntu 24.04:

wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2404/x86_64/cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb sudo dpkg -i cuda-keyring_1.1–1_all.deb sudo apt update

Install CUDA 12.9 (the minimum version that supports sm_120 in nvcc and aligns with available NCCL packages):

sudo apt install -y cuda-toolkit-12–9

Add CUDA 12.9 to your PATH. Append these to ~/.bashrc:

export PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.9/bin:$PATH export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.9/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

Reload and verify:

source ~/.bashrc nvcc -version

Expected output:

Cuda compilation tools, release 12.9, V12.9.86

System Build Dependencies

Install the full development stack. Most of these will already be present on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04:

sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake git curl wget ninja-build \ python3-dev python3-pip python3-venv \ libopenblas-dev libblas-dev liblapack-dev \ libjpeg-dev libpng-dev gcc g++ gfortran

For NCCL, install the version matching CUDA 12.9:

sudo apt install -y libnccl2 libnccl-dev

Note: if you are building for single-GPU use only (which is the common case for most researchers), you can skip NCCL entirely by setting USE_NCCL=0 during the build. This significantly reduces build complexity and is the recommended approach unless you are running multi-GPU distributed training.

Creating the Python Environment

Use a plain Python venv rather than conda for the build. Conda introduces its own library paths that can conflict with the system CUDA toolkit during compilation:

python3 -m venv ~/torch5090 source ~/torch5090/bin/activate pip install -upgrade pip setuptools wheel ninja cmake

If you have conda installed (Miniconda or Anaconda), it will re-activate its base environment every time you source .bashrc. Deactivate it explicitly after activating your venv:

source ~/torch5090/bin/activate conda deactivate

Your prompt should show only (torch5090), not (torch5090) (base).

Cloning PyTorch

Clone the main branch with all submodules. The recursive clone is not optional — PyTorch depends on dozens of third-party libraries (FBGEMM, XNNPACK, pybind11, protobuf, etc.) that live as git submodules:

git clone -recursive https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch ~/pytorch cd ~/pytorch git submodule sync git submodule update -init -recursive

The submodule sync step updates the submodule URLs in case any have moved since the last commit. Without it, submodule updates can silently fail and leave you with empty third-party directories that cause missing header errors deep in the build.

Install Python build requirements inside your venv:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Build Environment Variables

These variables control exactly what gets compiled. Set them all before starting the build:

export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.9 export PATH=$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$CUDA_HOME/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH export TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=”12.0" export CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$(python -c ‘import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_paths()[“purelib”])’) export USE_CUDA=1 export USE_NCCL=0 export USE_DISTRIBUTED=0 export USE_CUDNN=1 export USE_FLASH_ATTENTION=0 export USE_MEM_EFF_ATTENTION=0 export MAX_JOBS=4

The critical variables:

• —1 tells nvcc to compile kernels specifically for sm_120. Without this, the build will either compile for a default list that excludes sm_120, or try to compile for every architecture and massively increase build time.

• —2 flash attention compiles hundreds of CUDA kernel variants and is extremely memory hungry. Each nvcc invocation can consume 3–4 GB RAM. With MAX_JOBS=4 and flash attention enabled you easily hit 16+ GB just from compiler processes, causing OOM kills (exit code 137).

• —3 limits parallel ninja jobs. Counter-intuitively, more jobs causes OOM kills on CUDA compilation. 4 jobs with 7–8 GB each is stable on a 30 GB system. Adjust based on your available RAM.

• —4 disables multi-GPU communication libraries. For single-GPU workloads these add build time and complexity with no benefit.

Building PyTorch

Clean any previous failed build artifacts first. Stale CMake cache from a previous attempt against a different CUDA version will cause the new build to silently use wrong paths:

python setup.py clean rm -rf build

Start the build. Use nohup and background it so a terminal disconnect does not kill the process — this build takes 1 to 3 hours:

nohup pip install -v -no-build-isolation . > ~/pytorch_build.log 2>&1 & echo “Build PID: $!”

Monitor progress in real time:

tail -f ~/pytorch_build.log

Check if it is still running:

ps aux | grep pip

If the build fails, get the actual error rather than the generic pip error message:

grep -i “error\|fatal\|failed” ~/pytorch_build.log | grep -v “^-” | tail -30

Common Build Failures and Their Causes

Exit code 137 on CUDA files

OOM kill. The Linux kernel is killing individual nvcc processes because they consume too much RAM. Reduce MAX_JOBS and set USE_FLASH_ATTENTION=0.

nvcc fatal: Unsupported gpu architecture ‘compute_120’

Your CUDA toolkit is too old. CUDA 12.8 is the minimum for sm_120 support. CUDA 12.9 is recommended.

NCCL linker errors

Version mismatch between libnccl and your CUDA toolkit. Either install NCCL built for your exact CUDA version, or set USE_NCCL=0.

Missing headers in third_party/

Submodule initialization was incomplete. Run git submodule update -init -recursive again from inside ~/pytorch.

Terminated (no error message)

The WSL session was closed or the machine went to sleep. This is why nohup is essential. Restart the build — CMake will resume from where it stopped if you do not clean.

Verifying the Build

A successful build ends with:

Successfully built torch Successfully installed torch-2.12.0a0+gitfd1d1b0

Verify that sm_120 kernels are actually being executed:

python -c “ import torch print(‘PyTorch version:’, torch.__version__) print(‘CUDA available:’, torch.cuda.is_available()) print(‘CUDA version:’, torch.version.cuda) print(‘GPU:’, torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)) print(‘Compute capability:’, torch.cuda.get_device_capability(0)) a = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device=’cuda’) b = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device=’cuda’) c = torch.matmul(a, b) torch.cuda.synchronize() print(‘Matrix multiply: PASSED’) “

Expected output:

PyTorch version: 2.12.0a0+gitfd1d1b0 CUDA available: True CUDA version: 12.9 GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Compute capability: (12, 0) Matrix multiply: PASSED

Compute capability (12, 0) confirms sm_120. The matrix multiply executing without error confirms the Blackwell kernels are present and running.

Daily Workflow

Add a shell alias so activation is a single command. Append to ~/.bashrc:

alias torch-gpu=’source ~/torch5090/bin/activate && conda deactivate’

Set your default WSL user so WSL opens directly without requiring su -. Run this once in Windows PowerShell:

ubuntu config -default-user yourusername

Your complete daily startup becomes:

# Open WSL terminal torch-gpu
# activate environment cd ~/your-project
# go to project code . OR cursor .
# open editor

For the editor to connect properly to WSL, always open it from inside WSL using code . or cursor ., not by opening a Windows folder path. This ensures the editor’s terminal, Python interpreter, and file system all operate inside WSL with native I/O performance rather than crossing the Windows/WSL filesystem boundary.

Summary: What Actually Matters

CUDA version: 12.8 minimum, 12.9 recommended. CUDA 12.0 (Ubuntu apt default) and CUDA 12.6 do not support sm_120.

NCCL: Skip it (USE_NCCL=0) for single-GPU setups. Version mismatches are a common build failure source.

Flash attention: Disable during build (USE_FLASH_ATTENTION=0) to avoid OOM kills. Add it back separately once the base build works.

MAX_JOBS: 4 is safe for 30 GB RAM. More parallel jobs causes OOM kills on CUDA compilation.

Submodules: Always use -recursive clone and run submodule sync + update. Missing submodules cause cryptic missing header errors.

Build artifacts: Always clean (python setup.py clean && rm -rf build) before retrying after a failed build against a different CUDA version.

The RTX 5090 is a genuinely powerful GPU for research workloads. The setup friction is real but it is a one-time cost. Once the build is done, everything downstream — torchvision, huggingface, custom CUDA extensions — works normally against this installation.

items.title: Beyond the Stereotype: A Man’s Journey to Authentic Connection
items.content:
A Personal Exploration of Identity, Relationships, and Being Seen for Who You Really Are

Table of Contents

Foreword

Part I: The Weight of Being “A Man”

  • Chapter 1: The Invisible Individual
  • Chapter 2: Carrying Ghosts of Other People’s Stories
  • Chapter 3: The Suffocating Script

Part II: The Complexity of Connection

  • Chapter 4: When Dreams Become Checklists
  • Chapter 5: The Misunderstood Pause
  • Chapter 6: Building vs. Rushing

Part III: Breaking Through

  • Chapter 7: The Courage to Be Seen
  • Chapter 8: Rewriting the Narrative
  • Chapter 9: Love Without Assumptions

Epilogue: An Invitation

Foreword

In a world increasingly divided by generalizations and assumptions, one voice rises to say: “I am not a category. I am a person.” This book emerges from a place of raw honesty -a man’s plea to be seen, understood, and connected with as an individual, not as a representative of his gender.

The pages that follow are not an argument or a defense. They are an invitation to look deeper, to question our assumptions, and to recognize the profound humanity that exists beyond the labels we so readily assign.

Part I: The Weight of Being “A Man”

Chapter 1: The Invisible Individual

“Yes, I am a man. But before I am a man, I am me.”

The moment someone learns I’m a man, something shifts. Not always visibly, not always dramatically, but it shifts nonetheless. Suddenly, I’m not just a person with thoughts, feelings, dreams, and fears I’m a representative of an entire gender. I carry the weight of every disappointing relationship, every broken promise, every stereotype that has been reinforced by the actions of others who happen to share my gender.

But here’s what I want you to understand: my “manness” is just one facet of who I am. It’s like being asked to represent all people with brown eyes, or everyone born in October, or all individuals who prefer coffee over tea. The biological fact of my gender doesn’t predetermine my capacity for empathy, my communication style, or my approach to relationships.

The Research Behind Gender Assumptions

Recent studies in social psychology reveal the extent to which gender stereotypes shape our perceptions before we even begin to know someone as an individual. Dr. Susan Fiske’s research on social cognition shows that we form impressions within milliseconds of meeting someone, and gender is one of the primary categories our brains use to organize these first impressions.

A 2023 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that men reported feeling “pre-judged” in romantic contexts 73% more often than women, often feeling they had to overcome negative assumptions before being seen as individuals. The study noted that participants frequently described feeling like they were “auditioning against the mistakes of other men.”

This phenomenon, which researchers term “representational burden,” creates a unique psychological pressure. Unlike stereotypes that might advantage someone, the expectation to overcome negative assumptions before being seen as an individual creates what psychologist Dr. Michael Addis calls “defensive authenticity”- the exhausting process of constantly proving you’re different from the stereotype while simultaneously trying to be genuinely yourself.

The Personal Cost of Collective Judgment

When I walk into a room, when I start a conversation, when I express interest in someone - I’m not just bringing myself. I’m apparently bringing the collective disappointments of every man who came before me. This invisible baggage shapes interactions in ways that feel both unfair and exhausting.

I remember a conversation where I mentioned I enjoyed cooking. The response was immediate: “Oh, you’re one of the good ones.” While meant as a compliment, it stung. It implied that enjoying cooking made me exceptional among men, when in reality, it’s just something I happen to love. It reduced my individuality to a deviation from an expected norm.

This constant comparison to a negative baseline means that authentic expressions of who I am get filtered through a lens of gender expectations. If I’m thoughtful, I’m “not like other men.” If I take time to process emotions, I’m “actually sensitive.” If I prioritize emotional connection, I’m “mature for a man.”

Each of these comments, while potentially well-intended, reinforces the very stereotypes they seem to challenge. They suggest that these qualities are somehow unusual or unexpected in men, rather than recognizing them as human qualities that exist across all genders.

The Paradox of Proving Individuality

There’s a cruel irony in having to prove you’re an individual. The very act of trying to demonstrate that you don’t fit a stereotype can feel like you’re reinforcing its power. It’s like being asked to prove you’re not thinking of a pink elephant, the effort itself makes the elephant more present.

I find myself in conversations where I want to say, “I know you’ve been hurt before. I know other men have disappointed you. But I am not them. I am not the cumulative effect of their choices. I am here, in this moment, as myself, hoping to be known for who I actually am.”

But saying this out loud feels defensive, even when it comes from a place of genuine desire for connection. So instead, I try to show through actions, through consistency, through presence , hoping that over time, the individual will emerge from behind the shadow of the collective.

Moving Beyond the Representative Role

The path forward isn’t about rejecting the fact that I’m a man or pretending gender doesn’t matter. It’s about expanding the conversation beyond gender as a primary organizing principle for understanding someone’s character, values, and potential for connection.

What if, instead of starting with assumptions about what men are like, we started with curiosity about what this particular person is like? What if we approached each interaction as an opportunity to discover something new, rather than to confirm something we think we already know?

This shift requires effort from all of us. It means catching ourselves when we’re about to attribute someone’s behavior to their gender rather than their individual personality. It means asking questions instead of making assumptions. It means being willing to be surprised.

Chapter 2: Carrying Ghosts of Other People’s Stories

“I don’t want to be seen through past disappointments with someone else. I don’t want to carry wounds I didn’t cause.”

There’s a particular kind of loneliness that comes from being held responsible for pain you didn’t cause. It’s the experience of walking into a relationship carrying the ghosts of other people’s stories , expectations shaped by past hurts, defensive walls built against previous disappointments, and assumptions forged in the fire of old betrayals.

I understand why these defenses exist. Trust, once broken, doesn’t easily mend. Hearts, once wounded, develop sophisticated protection mechanisms. But what happens when those mechanisms become so automatic that they prevent new connections from forming? What happens when the ghosts of past relationships become more present than the living person standing in front of you?

The Inheritance of Past Hurt

In every new connection, there’s an invisible inheritance ceremony taking place. Along with the excitement of possibility and the hope of something beautiful, there’s often a transfer of old wounds, unprocessed disappointments, and defensive strategies developed in previous relationships.

I’ve found myself in conversations where I could sense the presence of these ghosts , the echo of someone who said they’d call but didn’t, the shadow of someone who made promises they couldn’t keep, the residue of someone who couldn’t handle emotional depth. These past experiences hover in the space between us, influencing reactions and interpretations in ways that have nothing to do with who I actually am or how I’m actually showing up.

Dr. Sue Johnson, the developer of Emotionally Focused Therapy, describes this phenomenon as “negative cycles” that can form when past attachment injuries influence present interactions. Her research shows that unresolved hurts from previous relationships create what she calls “raw spots”, areas of heightened sensitivity where current partner’s actions get interpreted through the lens of past pain.

A 2022 study in the Journal of Marriage and Family found that individuals who carried unresolved hurt from previous relationships were 2.3 times more likely to misinterpret neutral behaviors as potentially threatening or dismissive. The study noted that this hypervigilance, while understandable as a protective mechanism, often created the very distance and conflict it was designed to prevent.

The Burden of Collective Masculinity

As a man entering into connections with others, I often find myself carrying not just the ghosts of specific past relationships, but the broader cultural narrative about men and relationships. These stories are everywhere, in movies where men are emotionally unavailable, in songs about heartbreak caused by men who couldn’t commit, in conversations where men are described as fundamentally incapable of emotional depth.

These narratives create a kind of preemptive defensiveness. Before I’ve even had the chance to demonstrate my own capacity for emotional connection, I’m often interacting with someone who’s already braced for disappointment. It’s like trying to build trust while someone is waiting for you to prove the negative expectation right.

I remember a conversation where someone said, “I’m just waiting for you to get bored and leave like all the others.” The pain in their voice was real, and I understood it came from genuine hurt. But I also felt the weight of being presumed guilty of crimes I hadn’t committed. How do you build something new when the foundation is already cracked by expectations of failure?

The Exhaustion of Constant Proving

There’s a particular exhaustion that comes from feeling like you’re constantly auditioning against negative expectations. Every interaction becomes a performance designed to demonstrate that you’re different, that you’re safe, that you won’t be another source of disappointment.

This dynamic creates what psychologists call “emotional labor inequality”, where one person is constantly working to prove their worthiness while the other remains in a protective stance, waiting to be convinced. While this makes sense as a short-term protective strategy, it can become problematic when it extends indefinitely.

The irony is that this constant need to prove oneself can actually interfere with authentic connection. When someone is focused on demonstrating that they’re not like “all the others,” they may inadvertently become less genuinely themselves. The effort to overcome assumptions can overshadow the natural unfolding of personality and connection.

Research by Dr. Brené Brown on vulnerability shows that authentic connection requires what she calls “rumbling with vulnerability”, the willingness to show up as imperfect humans rather than as perfect representatives of our best intentions. But when someone is carrying the burden of others’ past hurt, this kind of vulnerable authenticity becomes much more difficult.

The Stories We Tell Ourselves

It’s important to acknowledge that this isn’t just about external projections. We all carry internal narratives shaped by our experiences, and men are not exempt from this process. The difference is that for men, these internal stories often get compounded by external assumptions in ways that can feel overwhelming.

I’ve noticed my own internal voice sometimes saying things like, “You need to be extra careful here because they’re probably expecting you to be emotionally unavailable,” or “Don’t mention that you need time to process this because they’ll think you’re being typical male and avoiding feelings.” These internal narratives, formed in response to external expectations, can create a kind of self-consciousness that interferes with natural interaction.

The challenge is learning to distinguish between reasonable caution based on someone’s actual words and actions, and defensive assumptions based on past hurt or cultural narratives. This requires a level of emotional intelligence and self-awareness that takes time to develop.

Breaking the Cycle

Breaking free from this dynamic requires conscious effort from all parties involved. It means recognizing when past hurt is influencing present perception. It means being willing to give someone the benefit of the doubt while also maintaining healthy boundaries. It means distinguishing between patterns that are actually emerging and patterns we’re afraid might emerge.

For those who have been hurt before, it means finding ways to remain open to new possibilities while honoring the wisdom gained from past experiences. It means learning to see protective mechanisms as temporary tools rather than permanent walls.

For those entering into connections with someone who carries past hurt, it means understanding that patience and consistency are not just nice gestures , they’re essential elements of healing and trust-building. It means recognizing that defensive reactions often aren’t about you, even when they’re directed at you.

The Gift of Starting Fresh

There’s something profoundly healing about being given the opportunity to start fresh, to be seen as who you are rather than who someone fears you might be. This doesn’t mean ignoring red flags or abandoning healthy caution. It means approaching each interaction with curiosity rather than predetermined conclusions.

When someone is willing to set aside their past disappointments long enough to genuinely get to know you, it creates space for something new to emerge. This kind of openness requires courage from both people, the courage to risk being hurt again, and the courage to show up authentically despite knowing that others may be watching for signs of familiar patterns.

Chapter 3: The Suffocating Script

“My ‘manness’ is not a script I follow.”

Society hands us scripts from the moment we’re born. For men, these scripts are particularly rigid and all-encompassing. Be strong. Don’t cry. Take charge. Don’t show weakness. Pursue aggressively. Don’t be too sensitive. The list goes on, creating a narrow corridor of acceptable behavior that many men find suffocating.

But what happens when you don’t fit the script? What happens when your natural personality, your genuine way of being in the world, doesn’t align with these predetermined expectations? What happens when you realize that following the script might make you acceptable to some, but it also makes you invisible to yourself?

The Invisible Cage

The masculine script is like an invisible cage, its bars are made of expectations rather than steel, but they can be just as confining. From childhood, boys learn what behaviors are rewarded and which ones are discouraged. The message is often subtle but consistent: your worth is tied to how well you perform masculinity, not how authentically you express your individual self.

Dr. Terry Real, a family therapist specializing in men’s issues, describes this as “socialized masculinity”, a set of cultural expectations that often conflicts with men’s natural emotional and relational capacities. His research shows that men who rigidly adhere to traditional masculine scripts report higher levels of depression, anxiety, and relationship dissatisfaction.

A landmark study published in Psychology of Men & Masculinity in 2023 found that men who felt pressure to conform to masculine stereotypes were 40% more likely to suppress their authentic emotional responses in relationships. The study noted that this suppression often led to partners feeling like they “didn’t really know” the men they were involved with.

The Performance vs. The Person

There’s a profound difference between performing masculinity and being yourself as someone who happens to be male. Performance requires constant monitoring, checking to make sure your responses align with expectations, suppressing impulses that don’t fit the script, amplifying traits that do.

I’ve watched men contort themselves to fit these expectations, and I’ve felt the pressure myself. The impulse to appear unaffected when you’re actually deeply moved. The tendency to offer solutions when what’s really needed is empathetic listening. The pressure to be certain when you’re actually still figuring things out.

But performance is exhausting, and it’s ultimately hollow. You might successfully project the image of what a man “should” be, but if that image doesn’t reflect who you actually are, the connections you form will be with your performance, not with you.

The Cost of Emotional Suppression

One of the most damaging aspects of the masculine script is the expectation that men should suppress or minimize their emotional experiences. This doesn’t just affect men, it affects everyone who tries to connect with them.

Research by Dr. Ronald Levant on “normative male alexithymia” shows that men are often socialized to be less aware of and less able to express their emotions. This isn’t a biological inevitability, it’s a learned response to cultural expectations. And it can be unlearned.

The irony is that emotional suppression, while seeming to make men “stronger” in some traditional sense, actually makes them less effective partners, friends, and leaders. Emotional intelligence, the ability to recognize, understand, and appropriately express emotions — is consistently linked to success in relationships and professional settings.

When I allow myself to feel deeply and express authentically, I’m not abandoning my masculinity, I’m claiming my humanity. The script might suggest that real men don’t get emotional about movies, or don’t need time to process difficult conversations, or don’t sometimes feel uncertain about big decisions. But real humans do all of these things.

The Pressure to Have All the Answers

Another suffocating aspect of the masculine script is the expectation that men should always know what they want, always have a plan, always be decisive. This creates enormous pressure to project certainty even when you’re genuinely uncertain.

In relationships, this can be particularly problematic. The script suggests that a “real man” would know immediately if he wants to marry someone, would have his life completely figured out, would never need time to think things through. But healthy decision-making, especially about significant life choices, often requires reflection, discussion, and time.

When I take time to really consider something important, whether it’s a career decision, a relationship milestone, or a major life change, it’s not because I’m wishy-washy or uncommitted. It’s because I take these things seriously enough to give them the thoughtful consideration they deserve.

The Authentic Alternative

The alternative to following the script isn’t chaos or self-indulgence, it’s authenticity. It’s the courage to show up as who you actually are, with your unique combination of strengths and vulnerabilities, certainties and questions, confidence and humility.

This might mean admitting when you don’t know something. It might mean expressing emotion in situations where the script says you should remain stoic. It might mean prioritizing connection over conquest, depth over breadth, quality over quantity.

Dr. Brené Brown’s research on wholehearted living shows that people who live authentically, who align their actions with their values rather than external expectations , report higher levels of life satisfaction, stronger relationships, and greater resilience in the face of challenges.

The Courage to Disappoint Expectations

Living authentically as a man often means being willing to disappoint people who are invested in you following the script. This can be particularly challenging because the script is often invisible, people may not even realize they’re expecting you to perform masculinity rather than simply be yourself.

Sometimes this means being vulnerable when others expect you to be invulnerable. Sometimes it means asking for support when others expect you to be self-sufficient. Sometimes it means saying “I don’t know” when others expect you to have all the answers.

The courage to disappoint these expectations is ultimately an act of service , both to yourself and to others. When you refuse to perform a role that doesn’t fit you, you give others permission to do the same. You model the possibility of authentic living in a world that often rewards performance over presence.

Creating New Scripts

The goal isn’t to eliminate all social expectations or to pretend that cultural context doesn’t matter. The goal is to expand the range of acceptable ways to be a man, to create space for individual variation within broader categories.

This means recognizing that masculinity isn’t a single way of being, it’s a broad spectrum that can include sensitivity and strength, thoughtfulness and decisiveness, vulnerability and confidence. It means understanding that you can be fully masculine while also being fully yourself.

The Checklist Mentality

The checklist mentality treats relationship milestones as achievements to be unlocked rather than natural expressions of deepening connection. It might sound like: “We should be exclusive by month three,” “I should meet your parents by month six,” “We should be engaged within two years.”

While timelines can be helpful for ensuring that relationships are progressing, they become problematic when they replace actual relationship development with the appearance of relationship development. You can check all the boxes and still not really know each other in the ways that matter most.

I’ve experienced conversations where it felt like the focus was more on securing certain outcomes than on genuinely getting to know each other. Where discussions about the future replaced curiosity about the present. Where the relationship became more about reaching predetermined milestones than about discovering what kind of connection was actually possible between us.

The Wedding Question

Wedding conversations can be particularly loaded in this regard. For many people, especially women, the wedding represents not just a celebration but a symbol of security, commitment, and social recognition. These are valid and important desires.

Instead of focusing on how to love each other better, how to navigate differences, how to support each other’s growth, the conversation becomes focused on an event.

The Paradox of Premature Planning

There’s a paradox in premature planning: the more you focus on securing a specific future outcome, the less attention you pay to building the kind of relationship that could actually support that outcome. It’s like being so focused on the destination that you forget to learn how to drive.

Real relationship development is messy and non-linear. It involves conflicts that need to be worked through, differences that need to be understood, individual growth that needs to be supported. It involves seeing each other in various contexts, under different stresses, in moments of both strength and vulnerability.

When the focus shifts too quickly to future planning, there’s a risk of missing these crucial development opportunities. You might find yourselves planning a wedding between two people who don’t yet know how to have difficult conversations, or who haven’t yet learned how to support each other through challenges.

Respect Through Patience

When I ask for time to really get to know someone before making major commitments, it’s not because I’m unsure about them , it’s because I take the commitment seriously enough to want to enter it with full awareness of what I’m promising.

I want to understand how we handle conflict, how we support each other’s dreams, how we navigate stress together. I want our commitment to be based on reality, not just hope.”

Dr. John Gottman’s research on successful long-term relationships emphasizes the importance of what he calls “building love maps” , detailed knowledge of your partner’s inner world, including their fears, dreams, values, and aspirations. This kind of deep knowing takes time to develop and can’t be rushed.

The Foundation Before the Building

Think of relationship development like constructing a building. You can have the most beautiful architectural plans in the world, but if you try to construct the upper floors before the foundation is solid, the entire structure will be unstable.

  • Deep emotional intimacy and trust
  • Effective communication and conflict resolution skills
  • Shared values and compatible life visions
  • Individual emotional health and maturity
  • Demonstrated ability to support each other through challenges

When these foundational elements are in place, conversations about the future feel natural and exciting. When they’re not yet developed, future planning can feel premature and pressure-filled.

One of the most valuable gifts we can give each other in relationships is presence , the ability to be fully engaged with where we are right now rather than constantly focused on where we’re going. This doesn’t mean never talking about the future, but it means making sure that future planning emerges from present connection rather than replacing it.

When I’m truly present with someone, I’m not thinking about timelines or milestones , I’m thinking about understanding them better, about sharing something meaningful, about deepening our connection in this moment. This presence creates the kind of intimacy that makes future planning feel natural and authentic rather than forced or premature.

Chapter 5: The Misunderstood Pause

“Sometimes, when I don’t immediately echo those talks, it’s not because I’m unsure about you. It’s because I take it seriously.”

There’s a particular kind of misunderstanding that happens in relationships around pacing and responsiveness. When someone shares their dreams, hopes, or desires for the future, there’s often an expectation of immediate reciprocation or enthusiasm. When that immediate response doesn’t come, it can be interpreted as disinterest, uncertainty, or emotional unavailability.

We live in a culture that often equates speed with sincerity. Fast responses are seen as enthusiastic, while slower responses are viewed with suspicion. But authentic emotional processing doesn’t always happen on demand. Sometimes the most genuine response requires time to formulate.

My first instinct is often to really take it in, to understand not just what they’re saying but what it means to them, to consider how I honestly feel about it rather than how I think I should feel about it.

Research in cognitive psychology shows that people process complex emotional information at different rates. Dr. Daniel Kahneman’s work on “thinking fast and slow” demonstrates that the most thoughtful responses often come from what he calls “System 2” thinking, the slower, more deliberate processing that allows for nuanced consideration of complex issues.

A 2022 study in the Journal of Communication found that individuals who took time to process before responding in important conversations were more likely to give responses that reflected their authentic feelings and values. The study noted that immediate responses were more likely to be influenced by social pressure or the desire to please rather than genuine sentiment.

The Misinterpretation of Thoughtfulness

Unfortunately, thoughtfulness is often misinterpreted in relationships. When someone takes time to process before responding to important topics, it can be seen as:

  • Lack of enthusiasm
  • Uncertainty about the relationship
  • Emotional unavailability
  • Preparing to disappoint
  • Being “typical” of their gender

But what if the pause actually represents:

  • Taking the topic seriously enough to give a thoughtful response
  • Respecting the importance of what was shared
  • Wanting to respond from an authentic place rather than a reactive one
  • Considering all the implications before making statements or commitments
  • Honoring both their own feelings and their partner’s by not rushing to conclusions

The Pressure to Perform Enthusiasm

There’s often significant pressure in relationships to immediately match someone’s energy and enthusiasm, especially around topics like future planning. This pressure can be well-intentioned , who doesn’t want to feel like their partner is excited about building a future together?

But performed enthusiasm is different from authentic enthusiasm. When someone feels pressured to immediately echo excitement about something before they’ve had time to genuinely consider it, the response might be enthusiastic in tone but hollow in substance.

I’ve learned that my authentic enthusiasms are worth waiting for. When I’m genuinely excited about something, when I’ve had time to really consider it and connect with it emotionally, my response is much more meaningful than any reflexive agreement could be.

Dr. Brené Brown’s research on authenticity shows that genuine emotional responses, even when they’re not immediately positive, create stronger relationship bonds than responses that are designed to please but don’t reflect authentic feeling.

The Different Languages of Caring

People express caring in different ways, and these differences can sometimes be misunderstood. Some people express caring through immediate emotional mirroring , when you’re excited, they get excited. When you’re worried, they get worried. This kind of responsiveness can feel very validating and connecting.

Other people express caring through thoughtful consideration , when you share something important, they want to really think about it, understand it fully, and respond in a way that honors the significance of what you’ve shared. This can sometimes feel less immediately validating but often leads to more substantive responses.

Neither approach is inherently better or worse, but misunderstandings arise when someone expects one style and receives another. The key is recognizing that different response styles can both reflect genuine caring and investment in the relationship.

The Fear Behind the Expectation

Often, the expectation for immediate enthusiastic responses comes from a place of fear or insecurity. Past experiences with people who were genuinely disinterested or uncommitted can create a hypersensitivity to any sign of hesitation or lack of immediate enthusiasm.

This is understandable and human. When you’ve been disappointed before, you develop radar for potential disappointment. The challenge is distinguishing between actual signs of disinterest and natural variations in processing and response style.

It’s worth considering: would you rather have someone immediately agree to something important without really thinking about it, or would you rather have someone take the time to consider it thoughtfully and then respond from a genuine place?

The Value of the Pause

The pause before responding to important relationship topics can actually be a sign of emotional maturity and relationship investment. It suggests:

  • The person takes the relationship seriously enough to think carefully before responding
  • They respect the importance of what was shared
  • They want their response to be authentic rather than reflexive
  • They’re considering not just their immediate reaction but the broader implications
  • They value honesty over people-pleasing

This doesn’t mean endless delays or avoidance , there’s a difference between thoughtful consideration and procrastination or avoidance. The key is communication about the process.

Bridging the Gap

The solution to this misunderstanding isn’t for everyone to respond at the same speed , it’s for better communication about different processing styles. When someone needs time to think about something important, they can say so. When someone is feeling anxious about a lack of immediate response, they can express that too.

“I want to give this the thought it deserves, so let me take some time to really consider it” is very different from just not responding. “I’m feeling a little anxious because I shared something important and I’m not sure how you’re feeling about it” creates space for connection rather than assumption.

The Deeper Yes

When someone takes time to really consider something important and then responds with genuine enthusiasm or commitment, that response carries more weight than an immediate reaction. It’s the difference between a reflexive yes and a considered yes , between agreeing to please someone and agreeing because you’ve genuinely connected with what they’re proposing.

The deeper yes is worth waiting for, both for the person giving it and the person receiving it. It represents a more solid foundation for future building than any amount of immediate enthusiasm that hasn’t been thoroughly considered.

Chapter 6: Building vs. Rushing

“So when I take time to know you deeply before I promise anything long-term, it’s not a lack of interest , it’s the highest form of respect I can offer. I want to build something real, not rushed.”

The Difference Between Timeline and Development

There’s an important distinction between following a timeline and following natural relationship development. A timeline is external , it’s based on social expectations, peer comparisons, or arbitrary deadlines. Development is internal , it’s based on how well you actually know each other, how effectively you communicate, how compatible your life visions are.

Timeline thinking sounds like: “We’ve been together six months, so we should be talking about moving in together.” Development thinking sounds like: “We’ve learned so much about each other and handle challenges well together , I’m excited to explore what deeper commitment might look like.”

The timeline approach treats relationship milestones as achievements to be unlocked at appropriate intervals. The development approach treats them as natural expressions of deepening connection and compatibility.

The Respect in Taking Time

When I tell someone I want to take time to really know them before making major commitments, I’m not expressing uncertainty about them, I’m expressing the depth of my respect for what we might build together. I’m saying that what we have is too important to rush, too valuable to risk on assumptions, too meaningful to base on hope alone.

This perspective requires a fundamental shift in how we think about relationship pacing. Instead of viewing slower movement as lack of enthusiasm, we can view it as recognition of significance. Instead of interpreting careful consideration as uncertainty, we can see it as commitment to getting things right.

A 2023 longitudinal study published in Developmental Psychology followed couples for seven years and found that those who took longer to reach major milestones (but still progressed steadily) reported higher relationship satisfaction and lower rates of major relationship problems. The researchers noted that “time spent in deep relationship development was never wasted time.”

What Real Building Looks Like

Real relationship building is often less dramatic than the movies suggest. It’s not always grand gestures and passionate declarations. More often, it’s the accumulation of small moments of understanding, connection, and demonstrated care.

It’s learning how someone handles stress and how you can best support them. It’s discovering their communication patterns and figuring out how to navigate differences effectively. It’s seeing how they treat others, how they handle responsibility, how they respond to your vulnerabilities.

It’s also the less romantic but equally important work of practical compatibility , understanding their relationship with money, their career ambitions, their family dynamics, their approaches to conflict resolution. These aren’t exciting topics for movies, but they’re crucial foundations for real life.

Dr. Eli Finkel’s research on relationship quality shows that modern marriages carry more emotional weight than ever before. We expect our partners to be not just companions but best friends, passionate lovers, co-parents, emotional supports, and intellectual equals. Meeting these expectations requires a level of compatibility and understanding that can only be developed through time and intentional attention.

The Courage of Honest Assessment

Taking time to really know someone requires the courage to see them clearly , not just their best qualities, but their limitations, their growth areas, their ways of being that might challenge you. It also requires the courage to be seen clearly yourself.

This kind of honest assessment isn’t about finding the “perfect” person, it’s about understanding what you’re actually choosing. Every person comes with both gifts and challenges. The question isn’t whether those challenges exist, but whether you understand them well enough to choose them consciously and whether you have the tools to navigate them together.

I’ve been in situations where I could sense that someone wanted me to fast-track to commitment before I felt like I really knew them. The pressure was often subtle but persistent , the suggestion that taking time meant lack of certainty, that someone who was “sure” would move faster.

But I’ve learned that premature certainty is often just an illusion created by infatuation, projection, or the desire for security. Real certainty , the kind that can support a lifetime commitment , comes from knowledge, not just feeling.

The Foundation Phases

Healthy relationship building tends to move through recognizable phases, though not necessarily in a linear fashion:

Discovery Phase: Learning about each other’s backgrounds, values, interests, and basic compatibility. This is often the most exciting phase because everything is new and possibilities seem endless.

Integration Phase: Beginning to see how you fit into each other’s actual lives , meeting friends and family, navigating different social contexts, handling minor conflicts and differences.

Reality Phase: Seeing each other under stress, during difficult times, when you’re not at your best. This phase tests whether your connection is strong enough to handle real-life challenges.

Commitment Phase: Having enough information and experience together to make informed decisions about deeper commitment. This is when major milestone conversations become natural rather than forced.

Rushing through these phases or skipping them entirely doesn’t eliminate the work they represent , it just postpones it until after major commitments have already been made.

The Security in Solid Foundation

Paradoxically, taking time to build a solid foundation actually creates more security than rushing to commitment. When you know you’ve been truly seen and chosen, when you’ve navigated challenges together successfully, when you’ve built effective communication patterns and demonstrated compatibility , that creates a much more solid sense of security than any timeline-based commitment could provide.

A relationship built on this kind of foundation doesn’t require constant reassurance because both people know it’s based on reality rather than hope or projection. You’re not wondering if your partner will still love you when they really get to know you , because they already do know you, and they’ve demonstrated their choice repeatedly.

When Building Feels Like Delay

The challenge with this approach is that building can sometimes feel like delay, especially when there’s social pressure or personal anxiety around timelines. It requires faith that the investment of time and attention will pay off, and tolerance for the uncertainty that comes with any developmental process.

It also requires clear communication about the process. The difference between “I need time to get to know you better” and “I’m not sure about you” is significant, but it’s not always obvious to the other person unless you explain it clearly.

The key is helping your partner understand that you’re building toward something, not away from it. That the time you’re taking is an investment in the relationship’s future strength, not a hedge against commitment.

The Gift of Patience

When two people are aligned on the value of building rather than rushing, it creates a unique kind of intimacy. You’re not performing for each other or trying to secure an outcome , you’re genuinely getting to know each other and letting something real develop.

This requires patience from both people , patience with the process, patience with uncertainty, patience with the fact that some of the most important things can’t be rushed. But this patience is ultimately a gift you give to each other and to the relationship itself.

Chapter 7: The Courage to Be Seen

“I just ask: please see me. Not a pattern. Talk with me, not at an image of past hurt.”

The request to be seen , really seen , is one of the most vulnerable asks we can make of another person. It’s asking them to set aside their assumptions, their past experiences, their defensive strategies, and their preconceptions long enough to encounter you as you actually are. It’s asking for something that requires enormous trust and courage from both people involved.

But what does it actually mean to be seen? And why is it so difficult to achieve in a world where we’re constantly being categorized, compared, and filtered through the lens of other people’s experiences?

The Difference Between Recognition and Seeing

Recognition is when someone identifies you as a type, a category, a familiar pattern. “Oh, you’re one of those guys who…” or “I’ve dated men like you before…” Recognition is quick, efficient, and often inaccurate. It’s based on surface similarities and previous experiences rather than present reality.

Seeing is different. Seeing requires slowing down, paying attention, asking questions, and being willing to be surprised. It’s the difference between recognizing a song you think you’ve heard before and actually listening to the lyrics, melody, and arrangement of the specific song that’s playing right now.

Dr. Martin Buber’s philosophical work on “I-Thou” relationships describes this distinction beautifully. He writes about the difference between relating to someone as an “It” , an object to be categorized and understood through previous frameworks — and relating to them as a “Thou”, a unique being worthy of direct encounter without preconception.

Research in social psychology supports this distinction. Studies show that when people approach others with what researchers call “cognitive flexibility” , the willingness to revise initial impressions based on new information , they form more accurate perceptions and develop stronger relationships.

The Barriers to Being Seen

Several factors make it difficult for people to truly see each other:

Past Hurt: When someone has been disappointed or betrayed before, they develop protective strategies that can interfere with clear perception. They might see threats where none exist or interpret neutral behaviors through the lens of past pain.

Social Conditioning: We’re taught to categorize people quickly based on gender, age, appearance, and other observable characteristics. These categories can be useful for social navigation but can also prevent us from seeing individual variation.

Cognitive Efficiency: Our brains are designed to process information quickly and efficiently. Pattern recognition and category-based thinking serve us well in many contexts, but they can create blind spots when it comes to understanding unique individuals.

Fear of Vulnerability: Truly seeing someone requires being open to having your assumptions challenged. It requires admitting that you might be wrong about someone, which can feel vulnerable and uncomfortable.

Time Pressure: Real seeing takes time and attention. In a culture that values speed and efficiency, the slow work of getting to know someone deeply can feel like a luxury rather than a necessity.

The Cost of Not Being Seen

When someone consistently experiences not being seen , being responded to as a category rather than as an individual , it creates a particular kind of loneliness. You can be surrounded by people who “know” you, who have opinions about you, who react to you, but who have never actually encountered the person you are beneath their assumptions.

This dynamic can lead to what psychologists call “identity foreclosure” , when someone starts to conform to others’ expectations of them because it’s easier than constantly fighting to be seen differently. Over time, the person might even lose touch with who they really are beneath the roles and stereotypes they’ve been assigned.

For men, this often means being seen primarily through the lens of masculinity rather than as complex individuals who happen to be male. The assumption might be that they’re emotionally unavailable, commitment-phobic, or primarily driven by physical rather than emotional connection , regardless of how they actually show up.

The Request for Fresh Eyes

When I ask to be seen rather than recognized, I’m asking for what we might call “fresh eyes” , the willingness to approach me as if you’re meeting me for the first time, regardless of your previous experiences with other men or your assumptions about how men typically behave.

This doesn’t mean ignoring red flags or abandoning healthy caution. It means being willing to gather actual evidence about who I am rather than relying on stereotypes or projections to fill in the gaps.

Fresh eyes involve:

  • Asking questions instead of making assumptions
  • Paying attention to how I actually behave rather than how you expect me to behave
  • Being willing to be surprised by aspects of my personality that don’t fit your previous experiences
  • Giving me space to show you who I am rather than testing me against predetermined criteria

The Challenge for Both Parties

Being truly seen requires vulnerability from the person asking to be seen, but it also requires courage from the person doing the seeing. When you agree to really see someone, you’re agreeing to:

  • Set aside your protective assumptions
  • Risk being wrong about your initial impressions
  • Invest time and emotional energy in getting to know someone
  • Be open to forming a connection with someone who might challenge your previous experiences
  • Question your own biases and defensive strategies

This is why the request to be seen is so significant , it’s asking for a level of openness and vulnerability from both people that goes far beyond casual interaction.

Creating Space for Authentic Encounter

True seeing requires creating the right conditions for authentic encounter. This means:

Slowing Down: Real seeing can’t be rushed. It requires taking time to notice details, ask follow-up questions, and allow complexity to emerge.

Suspending Judgment: This doesn’t mean abandoning discernment, but it means being willing to hold space for information that doesn’t fit your initial impressions.

Active Curiosity: Instead of waiting for someone to prove they’re different from your expectations, actively looking for evidence of who they actually are.

Present-Moment Awareness: Focusing on how someone is showing up right now rather than how people like them have shown up in the past.

Emotional Regulation: Managing your own triggered responses long enough to gather accurate information about the person in front of you.

The Intimacy of Being Seen

When someone truly sees you , when they encounter you as you actually are rather than as they expected you to be , it creates a unique form of intimacy. It’s the intimacy of being known, of having your individual humanity recognized and appreciated.

This kind of seeing is often what people are really looking for when they say they want to “be loved for who they are.” They want to be loved not despite their individuality but because of it , loved not as a representative of a category but as a unique person worthy of specific attention and care.

Dr. Sue Johnson’s research on attachment in adult relationships shows that feeling truly seen and understood by a partner is one of the strongest predictors of relationship satisfaction and security. When people feel like their partners really know them , not just their public persona but their inner world , they’re more likely to feel safe being vulnerable and authentic.

The Courage to Ask

Asking to be seen requires enormous courage because it involves several significant risks:

  • The risk that someone will refuse to really look at you
  • The risk that they’ll see you clearly and decide they’re not interested
  • The risk of being vulnerable with someone who might use that vulnerability against you
  • The risk of disappointment if someone agrees to see you but falls back into pattern-based thinking

But it also offers the possibility of something profound: the experience of being known and chosen for who you actually are rather than who someone thinks you should be.

The Gift Exchange

When someone agrees to really see you, and when you offer to be genuinely seen, you’re engaging in a profound gift exchange. You’re offering your authentic self, and they’re offering their undivided attention and openness. Both offerings require courage, and both create the possibility for real connection.

This exchange can’t be forced or negotiated , it has to be freely given and received. But when it happens, it creates the foundation for the kind of relationship where both people can be fully themselves without fear of being reduced to stereotypes or categories.
